Reference: Gowrisankaran and Rysman (2012)

Model Setting

New consumer durables show rapidly falling prices and rising quality, so when to buy matters as much as what to buy. The paper nests a random-coefficient logit demand system in the style of Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995, BLP) inside an optimal-stopping problem in the style of Rust (1987): consumers with persistently heterogeneous tastes hold at most one product, form rational expectations about future prices and qualities, and may repurchase (upgrade) at any time. The estimation uses only product-level data on prices, sales and characteristics. The key device is the logit inclusive value: the whole industry state enters the consumer's problem only through one scalar, and consumers are assumed to forecast that scalar with a first-order autoregression. This reduces the dynamic problem to two state variables per consumer type and avoids solving the supply side. The model is estimated on monthly data for digital camcorders in the United States from March 2000 to May 2006, a period in which average prices fell from 930 to 380 dollars, average pixel counts rose from 580,000 to 1.08 million, and the number of models grew from fewer than 30 to almost 100.

The dynamic estimates are sensible (a log-price coefficient of −3.30-3.30−3.30 and positive valuations of most characteristics), whereas a static BLP model on the same data gives a price coefficient of −0.099-0.099−0.099 with a standard error of 148 and many wrong-signed characteristics. The authors' explanation is that a durable purchase is an investment decision: what matters is the rental cost, roughly pt−βpt+1p_t-\beta p_{t+1}pt​−βpt+1​, and not the price level, and the pool of remaining buyers deteriorates as high-value consumers leave the market. A temporary industry-wide price increase of 1 percent lowers sales in that month by 2.55 percent, but 44 percent of the lost sales return within 12 months, and a permanent increase lowers sales by only 1.23 percent. A dynamic cost-of-living index rises by 1.27 dollars per household per month over the sample, against 1.74 dollars for a BLS-style index, because later buyers value the good less than early buyers.

Consumer Problem

The industry starts at t=0t=0t=0. A consumer lives forever, discounts at factor β\betaβ, benefits from at most one camcorder at a time (Leontief usage), and there is no resale market, so an old unit is costlessly discarded on replacement. In period ttt there are models j=1,…,Jtj=1,\ldots,J_tj=1,…,Jt​, each with net flow utility fjtf_{jt}fjt​ and price disutility PjtP_{jt}Pjt​. Buying model jjj gives utility in period ttt of:

ujt=fjt−Pjt+εjtforj=1,…,Jt(1)u_{jt}=f_{jt}-P_{jt}+\varepsilon_{jt}\qquad\text{for}\quad j=1,\ldots,J_t \tag{1}ujt​=fjt​−Pjt​+εjt​forj=1,…,Jt​(1)

and not buying gives:

u0t=f0t+ε0t(2)u_{0t}=f_{0t}+\varepsilon_{0t} \tag{2}u0t​=f0t​+ε0t​(2)

where εjt\varepsilon_{jt}εjt​ and ε0t\varepsilon_{0t}ε0t​ are type 1 extreme value shocks, i.i.d. across models and periods, and f0tf_{0t}f0t​ is the flow utility of the product currently owned. A consumer who has never bought holds the outside good with f0t=0f_{0t}=0f0t​=0. After a purchase of model j^\hat{j}j^​ at time t^\hat{t}t^, f0tf_{0t}f0t​ equals fj^t^f_{\hat{j}\hat{t}}fj^​t^​ in every later period until the next purchase. The consumer therefore needs to remember only one number, the flow utility of the most recent purchase, and not the identity of the product. Price is paid once, while flow utility accrues every month.

Inclusive Value Sufficiency

Ω\OmegaΩ is far too large to carry as a state. The aggregation property of the extreme value distribution collapses the inner maximum (Euler's constant is dropped):

V(f0,Ω)=ln⁡[exp⁡(f0+βE[V(f0,Ω′)∣Ω])+exp⁡(δ(Ω))](4)V(f_0,\Omega)=\ln\left[\exp\left(f_0+\beta E\left[V(f_0,\Omega')\mid\Omega\right]\right)+\exp\left(\delta(\Omega)\right)\right] \tag{4}V(f0​,Ω)=ln[exp(f0​+βE[V(f0​,Ω′)∣Ω])+exp(δ(Ω))](4)

where the logit inclusive value is:

δ(Ω)=ln⁡[∑j=1,…,Jexp⁡(fj−Pj+βE[V(fj,Ω′)∣Ω])](5)\delta(\Omega)=\ln\left[\sum_{j=1,\ldots,J}\exp\left(f_j-P_j+\beta E\left[V(f_j,\Omega')\mid\Omega\right]\right)\right] \tag{5}δ(Ω)=ln​j=1,…,J∑​exp(fj​−Pj​+βE[V(fj​,Ω′)∣Ω])​(5)

δ(Ω)\delta(\Omega)δ(Ω) is the ex ante discounted lifetime value of buying the preferred available model. The value function is therefore the same as in a simpler problem in which the consumer either keeps her product or makes a purchase of a single composite good with mean utility δ(Ω)\delta(\Omega)δ(Ω). Ω\OmegaΩ matters only through the current δ\deltaδ and through the forecast of future δ\deltaδ. Unlike the inclusive values in Melnikov (forthcoming) and Hendel and Nevo (2006), which are built from flow utilities alone, this δ\deltaδ contains the continuation values E[V(fj,Ω′)∣Ω]E[V(f_j,\Omega')\mid\Omega]E[V(fj​,Ω′)∣Ω], so it reflects that the buyer of a better model is less likely to upgrade later. Let gδg_{\delta}gδ​ be the density of δ\deltaδ. The central assumption is inclusive value sufficiency (IVS):

δ(Ω)=δ(Ω~)  ⟹  gδ(δ(Ω′)∣Ω)=gδ(δ(Ω~′)∣Ω~)for all Ω,Ω~(6)\delta(\Omega)=\delta(\tilde{\Omega})\;\Longrightarrow\;g_{\delta}\left(\delta(\Omega')\mid\Omega\right)=g_{\delta}\left(\delta(\tilde{\Omega}')\mid\tilde{\Omega}\right)\qquad\text{for all }\Omega,\tilde{\Omega} \tag{6}δ(Ω)=δ(Ω~)⟹gδ​(δ(Ω′)∣Ω)=gδ​(δ(Ω~′)∣Ω~)for all Ω,Ω~(6)

Proposition 1 states that under IVS, δ(Ω)=δ(Ω~)\delta(\Omega)=\delta(\tilde{\Omega})δ(Ω)=δ(Ω~) implies V(f0,Ω)=V(f0,Ω~)V(f_0,\Omega)=V(f_0,\tilde{\Omega})V(f0​,Ω)=V(f0​,Ω~). which depends on Ω\OmegaΩ only through δ\deltaδ. For earlier periods:

The second is equal because IVS gives the same distribution of δ′\delta'δ′ and the induction hypothesis makes VtTV^T_tVtT​ a function of δ′\delta'δ′ alone. Discounting and bounded characteristics allow the limit T→∞T\to\inftyT→∞. The state is then (f0,δ)(f_0,\delta)(f0​,δ), with reduced value function V\mathcal{V}V:

IVS is restrictive: a high δ\deltaδ may come from many expensive models or from one cheap model, and the consumer treats the two states as having the same future. The authors prefer to read it as a description of boundedly rational perceptions.

Expectations

Consumers have rational expectations within this limited-information rule: the perceived density gδ(δ′∣δ)g_{\delta}(\delta'\mid\delta)gδ​(δ′∣δ) is the empirical density fitted to a linear autoregression:

δt+1=γ1+γ2δt+νt+1(11)\delta_{t+1}=\gamma_1+\gamma_2\delta_t+\nu_{t+1} \tag{11}δt+1​=γ1​+γ2​δt​+νt+1​(11)

where νt+1\nu_{t+1}νt+1​ is normal with mean zero and unknown at ttt, and γ1,γ2\gamma_1,\gamma_2γ1​,γ2​ are incidental parameters obtained by regressing the realized sequence of δt\delta_tδt​ on its lag. Consumers are thus right on average about how fast the market improves. For 0<γ2<10<\gamma_2<10<γ2​<1 they expect δ\deltaδ to approach the asymptote γ1/(1−γ2)\gamma_1/(1-\gamma_2)γ1​/(1−γ2​), which acts as a long-run steady state and is how a stationary dynamic program represents an evolving industry. In the estimates the asymptote is reached long after the sample ends. Proposition 2 shows that, with a finite set of industry states, any set of transition probabilities for δ\deltaδ can be rationalized by some process for the underlying fjf_jfj​ and PjP_jPj​ (the proof uses Schauder's fixed-point theorem and the fact that flow utilities and prices have higher dimension than δ\deltaδ). The alternative specification is perfect foresight, in which consumers know all future fjf_jfj​ and PjP_jPj​ and the industry state is simply ttt.

Optimal behavior is the joint solution of three objects: the reduced Bellman equation, the definition of δ\deltaδ, and the autoregression. Solving the Bellman equation alone is not enough, because a different value function implies different δt\delta_tδt​, hence different γ1,γ2\gamma_1,\gamma_2γ1​,γ2​, hence a different Bellman equation. Appendix B checks the approximation in a one-product example with constant price in which the flow utility, not δ\deltaδ, is autoregressive:

ft+1=0.0005+0.99ft+νt+1,ν∼N(0,0.002)(12)f_{t+1}=0.0005+0.99f_t+\nu_{t+1},\qquad\nu\sim N(0,0.002) \tag{12}ft+1​=0.0005+0.99ft​+νt+1​,ν∼N(0,0.002)(12)

with P=5P=5P=5, β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99 and initial f=−0.04f=-0.04f=−0.04. If the consumer had to keep the product forever, its value net of price would be:

f1−β−P(13)\frac{f}{1-\beta}-P \tag{13}1−βf​−P(13)

and δ\deltaδ lies above this value because it includes the option to upgrade, with a gap that shrinks over time. The long-run mean of fff is 0.05, so the net value tends to zero (the paper attaches the figure 0.05 to the net value, which is loose). Market shares of a consumer who uses the misspecified autoregression for δ\deltaδ are very close to those of a consumer who knows the true process.

This is where the model departs from static BLP: the composition of potential buyers changes endogenously, because high-value types buy early and afterwards face a higher f0f_0f0​. The market size is the number of US households.

The supply side is not solved. Models arrive and their characteristics evolve exogenously; firms observe consumer holdings, xjtx_{jt}xjt​ and ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ and set prices simultaneously in a Markov-perfect equilibrium without commitment. Prices may therefore be correlated with ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​, while characteristics are not. These assumptions suffice for demand estimation, but counterfactuals that change the industry equilibrium would need a full dynamic oligopoly model.

Estimation: Nested Fixed Points

The discount factor is not estimated, since it is poorly identified (Magnac and Thesmar 2002): waiting can be explained by patience or by moderate tastes. It is set to β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99 per month, leaving (α,Σ)(\alpha,\Sigma)(α,Σ). The estimator has three layers. The outer layer is GMM on the moments:

G(α,Σ)=z′ξ⃗(α,Σ)(19)G(\alpha,\Sigma)=z'\vec{\xi}(\alpha,\Sigma) \tag{19}G(α,Σ)=z′ξ​(α,Σ)(19)
(α^,Σ^)=arg⁡min⁡α,Σ{G(α,Σ)′WG(α,Σ)}(20)\left(\hat{\alpha},\hat{\Sigma}\right)=\arg\min_{\alpha,\Sigma}\left\{G(\alpha,\Sigma)'WG(\alpha,\Sigma)\right\} \tag{20}(α^,Σ^)=argα,Σmin​{G(α,Σ)′WG(α,Σ)}(20)

where zzz is a matrix of exogenous variables, WWW a weighting matrix, and ξ⃗(α,Σ)\vec{\xi}(\alpha,\Sigma)ξ​(α,Σ) the vector of unobserved characteristics that equates predicted and observed shares. As in Nevo (2000), αx\alpha^xαx is concentrated out by linear algebra, so the nonlinear search is over αp\alpha^pαp and Σ\SigmaΣ only. The middle layer finds the mean flow utilities F⃗\vec{F}F that solve the share equations:

sjt=s^jt(F⃗,αp,Σ)∀j,t(21)s_{jt}=\hat{s}_{jt}(\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)\qquad\forall j,t \tag{21}sjt​=s^jt​(F,αp,Σ)∀j,t(21)

by an analogue of the BLP contraction:

Fjtnew=Fjtold+ψ⋅{ln⁡(sjt)−ln⁡[s^jt(F⃗old,αp,Σ)]}∀j,t(22)F^{\text{new}}_{jt}=F^{\text{old}}_{jt}+\psi\cdot\left\{\ln(s_{jt})-\ln\left[\hat{s}_{jt}(\vec{F}^{\text{old}},\alpha^p,\Sigma)\right]\right\}\qquad\forall j,t \tag{22}Fjtnew​=Fjtold​+ψ⋅{ln(sjt​)−ln[s^jt​(Fold,αp,Σ)]}∀j,t(22)

with tuning parameter ψ\psiψ generally set to 1−β1-\beta1−β. A natural reading of the damping is that FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ is a monthly flow while shares respond to its discounted sum. Two things change relative to static BLP. The inversion cannot be done market by market, since FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ in one month affects δit\delta_{it}δit​, holdings and therefore shares in all months. And the mapping is not known to be a contraction: with repurchase, products in different periods can be complements (a lower price today reduces sales next period but can raise sales two periods ahead as more consumers find an upgrade worthwhile), so the uniqueness argument of Berry (1994) fails. The authors always converge to the same solution from different starting values and impose uniqueness of F⃗\vec{F}F as Assumption 2. The inner layer, for each simulated consumer type, solves the reduced Bellman equation, the inclusive value and the autoregression jointly. In practice the layers are not fully nested: starting from guesses of δit\delta_{it}δit​, Vi(fi0t,δit)\mathcal{V}_i(f_{i0t},\delta_{it})Vi​(fi0t​,δit​) and FjtF_{jt}Fjt​, the algorithm cycles through the equations by successive approximation, taking only a few iterations of each before moving on, until all converge. Then ξjt=Fjt−xjtαx\xi_{jt}=F_{jt}-x_{jt}\alpha^xξjt​=Fjt​−xjt​αx enters the GMM objective. Dube, Fox and Su (2012) propose the MPEC alternative, which Conlon (2010) applied to a variant of this model.

The estimation uses 40 importance draws built from Halton sequences, and 100 draws do not change the base results. The paper reports standard errors but does not describe how they are computed. The non-nested tests below use first-stage GMM estimates.

Identification and Instruments

The dynamic model adds no parameters to static BLP other than the fixed β\betaβ. The response of a model's share to its characteristics identifies α\alphaα, and the products from which it draws share identify Σ\SigmaΣ: proportional substitution implies small Σ\SigmaΣ, substitution toward similar products implies large Σ\SigmaΣ. The dynamic model also uses substitution across periods: an unusually cheap low-quality model early in the sample removes consumers with a taste for such models from later demand. Price is endogenous to ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ and characteristics are exogenous. The instruments zzz are BLP-style variables that shift margins and not costs: the characteristics xxx, mean characteristics of the same firm's models in the period, mean characteristics of all models in the period, and the number of models offered by the firm and by all firms. Sales data alone cannot tell first purchases from upgrades, so the extent of repeat purchase is not pinned down directly, although the model is formally identified. One specification therefore adds a micro moment in the manner of Petrin (2002): the model's increase in household penetration between September 2002 and September 2005 must match the survey figure. The growth of ownership relative to sales over that window pins down the extent of repurchase.

Data

The main data are a monthly panel from NPD Techworld, which covers about 80 percent of the market, with units sold, average price and characteristics for 383 models of 11 brands. Model-months with fewer than 100 units, or prices below 100 or above 2,000 dollars, are dropped, leaving 4,436 observations on 343 models. The number of models rises from 29 to 98, and the median model stays in the data for 14 months. Characteristics are size (width times depth), pixels, zoom, LCD screen size, indicators for lamp, night shot and photo capability, and recording medium (tape, DVD, hard drive, memory card); continuous variables are in logs. Sales spike every December while prices do not, so sales are seasonally adjusted with month-of-year factors that equalize geometric mean sales across months and preserve total sales. An alternative specification keeps raw sales and adds month dummies to utility at the time of purchase, which requires month of the year as an extra state variable. Penetration comes from the ICR-CENTRIS telephone survey of about 4,000 households per month. It is noisy (in three of six years the rise in penetration exceeds new sales) and is used in one specification only.

Estimates

The tables report the coefficient on log price as it enters utility, which is negative. Read literally, u=f−Pu=f-Pu=f−P with P=αpln⁡(p)P=\alpha^p\ln(p)P=αpln(p) would call for a positive αp\alpha^pαp, so the reported number is −αp-\alpha^p−αp in the notation of the model. Characteristic coefficients are monthly flows and should be about 1−β=0.011-\beta=0.011−β=0.01 times their static counterparts, while price coefficients are directly comparable.

  • Base dynamic model: the mean log-price coefficient is −3.30-3.30−3.30 (standard error 1.03) with standard deviation 0.345 (0.115). The mean constant is −0.092-0.092−0.092 (0.029) with standard deviation 0.079 (0.021). Smaller size (−0.007-0.007−0.007), pixels (0.010), zoom (0.005), LCD size (0.003), lamp (0.005), night shot (0.003) and the DVD, tape and hard-drive dummies (0.033, 0.012, 0.036, relative to memory card) all have the expected sign and are significant. Only photo capability is wrong-signed (−0.007-0.007−0.007). All characteristic coefficients are smaller than the constant, so vertical differentiation among camcorders is small relative to the gap with the outside good.

  • No repurchase: restricting consumers to one purchase ever cuts the price coefficient to −0.543-0.543−0.543 (3.09), flips several signs, and gives negligible heterogeneity. A Rivers and Vuong (2002) test rejects it in favor of the base model with a statistic of 5.55. The base model predicts few repurchases, but with the single-purchase coefficients it would predict far too many.

  • Static BLP: the price coefficient is −0.099-0.099−0.099 (148), the constant −6.86-6.86−6.86 (358), and the pixel, LCD size and lamp coefficients are wrong-signed. The non-nested test statistic against the base model is 5.7.

  • Micro moment: the price coefficient is −3.43-3.43−3.43 (0.225), and its standard deviation more than doubles to 0.820 (0.084). Coefficients on the characteristics that improve most over time rise two- to threefold (size −0.021-0.021−0.021, pixels 0.027, zoom 0.018). The model generates repurchase through a group of price-insensitive consumers who care about improving features.

Robustness and Fit

Adding ln⁡(Jt)\ln(J_t)ln(Jt​) as a second state variable that predicts future inclusive values (two forecasting regressions in δ\deltaδ and ln⁡J\ln JlnJ) leaves the estimates almost unchanged (price −3.31-3.31−3.31), which supports IVS. Perfect foresight, with the market frozen after the last sample month, gives a price coefficient of −2.53-2.53−2.53 with essentially no price heterogeneity and the same qualitative results. Two extra random coefficients on size and pixels are small and insignificant (price −3.01-3.01−3.01). A linear-price specification and a specification with month dummies (price −3.06-3.06−3.06; December effect 0.720, the only significant one) are similar. Melnikov's model, with one purchase and no random coefficients, gives a small price coefficient of −0.189-0.189−0.189 (which the paper's text calls insignificant, although its table marks it as significant) and several negative characteristic coefficients. Including ln⁡(Jt)\ln(J_t)ln(Jt​) as a characteristic in FjtF_{jt}Fjt​, the Ackerberg and Rysman (2005) test for crowding, gives a coefficient of −0.013-0.013−0.013, close to the logit benchmark of zero. A quadratic time trend is economically unimportant.

Monthly averages of ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ show no autocorrelation or trend, although the model has no reduced-form device to fit the diffusion path. The inclusive values δit\delta_{it}δit​ rise almost linearly for all types, and heterogeneity in levels dominates the change over time: a consumer at the 20th percentile of both random coefficients values the market at the end of the sample far less than a consumer at the 80th percentile did at the start. The forecast errors of the autoregression are tested with the moment:

E[νitνit+1]=0(26)E\left[\nu_{it}\nu_{it+1}\right]=0 \tag{26}E[νit​νit+1​]=0(26)

which is not imposed in estimation; for the median consumer its sample value is −0.474-0.474−0.474 with standard deviation 2.95, so the null hypothesis of no serial correlation cannot be rejected. In the base model repeat purchases are only about 0.25 percent of sales in the last month, because the main heterogeneity is in the constant: buyers value having a camcorder but distinguish little between models. With the micro moment (an increase in penetration of 4.9 percent against new sales of 5.85 percent over the same three years), more than 25 percent of sales at the end of the sample are repeat purchases. Two simulations show the role of dynamics. If consumers believed the market would never improve, sales would decline somewhat over time instead of growing rapidly. If holdings were erased every period but consumers still regarded the good as durable when buying, sales would track the base case for about 2 years and then grow much faster, even though roughly 90 percent of households had not bought by the end of the sample.

Price Elasticities

Elasticities use the base estimates and an unexpected 1 percent price increase in the median month, April 2003. A temporary increase lasts one month and is known to be temporary, so the forecast of δi,t+1\delta_{i,t+1}δi,t+1​ is formed from the baseline δit\delta_{it}δit​. A permanent increase is known to be permanent, and the forecast uses the realized δit\delta_{it}δit​. In both cases γ1i\gamma_{1i}γ1i​ and γ2i\gamma_{2i}γ2i​ are held at their estimated values.

  • Industry-wide: sales in the month fall by 2.55 percent after a temporary increase and by 1.23 percent after a permanent one, about 48 percent as much. Consumers postpone when they expect prices to come back: 44 percent of the sales lost in month ttt are recovered over the next 12 months, so the one-year elasticity of a temporary change is 56 percent of the one-month elasticity.

  • Single model (Sony DCRTRV250, the largest seller that month): the responses are 2.59 percent and 2.41 percent. Temporary and permanent changes are alike because consumers switch to another model instead of waiting.

  • Comparison: the short-run temporary elasticity is almost the same for one model as for the industry, but for different reasons (substitution across models against substitution across time). Expectations about prices are therefore central to firms' pricing. The static model's elasticities are all close to zero.

Cost-of-Living Indices

The BLS-style price index ItI_tIt​ is a Laspeyres index, with the prices of exiting models imputed from the average price decline of continuing models:

It+1It=∑j=1Jtsjtpj,t+1∑j=1Jtsjtpjt(27)\frac{I_{t+1}}{I_t}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{J_t}s_{jt}p_{j,t+1}}{\sum_{j=1}^{J_t}s_{jt}p_{jt}} \tag{27}It​It+1​​=∑j=1Jt​​sjt​pjt​∑j=1Jt​​sjt​pj,t+1​​(27)

normalized to 100 in March 2000. It falls to 12.7 by May 2006. The index of Pakes (2003), which predicts the prices of exiting models from monthly hedonic regressions, falls to 14.5, so the new-goods bias is small. To express these as a cost-of-living index (COLI) per household, the outside good is added with a constant price, and the index is scaled by the initial share-weighted average price of 961 dollars and subtracted from that price. The result is the reduction in income that still lets a household buy the first-period basket. It reaches 1.74 dollars per household per month for the BLS version and 1.72 for the Pakes version; the numbers are small because market shares are small.

The dynamic COLI is a compensating variation computed with the linear-price specification (the paper cites column 3 of its robustness table, but linear price is column 4), so that money has a constant marginal utility. A planner sets taxes contingent on the aggregate state that keep average flow utility, and hence the average expected value function, constant over time; in the linear-price model such taxes do not alter purchases. A buyer of a model priced pjtp_{jt}pjt​ is treated as paying the amortized amount (1−β)pjt(1-\beta)p_{jt}(1−β)pjt​ in every later period, since otherwise the payments of new buyers would swamp the flow utility of owners. The dynamic COLI ends at 1.27 dollars. The three indices coincide for about two years and then diverge: the BLS index keeps rising roughly linearly with falling prices and rising sales, while the dynamic index is concave. This is the new buyer problem of Aizcorbe (2005): later buyers either have low valuations or already own a camcorder, so standard indices that treat demand as homogeneous over time overstate later welfare gains. A COLI from the static BLP estimates peaks at an implausible 6.92 dollars.

This is the period-ttt payoff from buying model jjj, for one consumer (the consumer index iii is added in equation (14)). The term fjtf_{jt}fjt​ is the net flow utility of the model per month, measured relative to the outside good, whose flow utility is normalized to zero. The term PjtP_{jt}Pjt​ is the disutility of the purchase price, that is, the utility lost because less of the money good is consumed; it enters with a minus sign, so a higher price means a larger PjtP_{jt}Pjt​. The shock εjt\varepsilon_{jt}εjt​ is type 1 extreme value, i.i.d. across models and months, and stands for transitory features of the shopping occasion.

Two points matter for what follows. First, ujtu_{jt}ujt​ is only the payoff in the month of purchase. The flow fjtf_{jt}fjt​ is received again in every later month in which the model is kept, while PjtP_{jt}Pjt​ is paid once. The full value of buying is therefore

which is the second branch of the Bellman equation (3). Second, the extreme value assumption is what delivers the closed forms later: the log-sum in equation (4), the inclusive value in equation (5) and the logit purchase probability in equation (16). Because the shock is i.i.d. over time, it creates no persistence; all persistence comes from the holding f0tf_{0t}f0t​ and, with heterogeneity, from the random coefficients in equation (14).

A rough special case: if the buyer never replaced the model, the value of buying would be fjt/(1−β)−Pjt+εjtf_{jt}/(1-\beta)-P_{jt}+\varepsilon_{jt}fjt​/(1−β)−Pjt​+εjt​, so one unit of monthly flow utility is worth 1/(1−β)=1001/(1-\beta)=1001/(1−β)=100 units of price disutility at β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99. This is why the estimated characteristic coefficients are about one hundredth of static ones.

This is the period-ttt payoff of a consumer who buys nothing. The term f0tf_{0t}f0t​ is the flow utility of whatever she currently holds. It equals 000 for a consumer who has never bought (she holds the outside good), and it equals fj^t^f_{\hat{j}\hat{t}}fj^​t^​, the flow utility of the most recent purchase, afterwards. The shock ε0t\varepsilon_{0t}ε0t​ is type 1 extreme value and i.i.d. over time, like the shocks in equation (1).

The equation carries three modelling choices. There is no depreciation: the flow utility of a held unit stays at its purchase-date value, including the purchase-date unobservable ξj^t^\xi_{\hat{j}\hat{t}}ξj^​t^​ of equation (14). There is no resale and no scrap value: the old unit simply disappears from the problem when a new one is bought. And usage is Leontief: only the most recent purchase yields utility. Together these imply that the consumer's own history is summarized by the single number f0tf_{0t}f0t​, which is the individual state variable in the Bellman equation (3) and in its reduced form (9).

This is Assumption 1 of the paper, inclusive value sufficiency (IVS). The object gδ(δ(Ω′)∣Ω)g_{\delta}(\delta(\Omega')\mid\Omega)gδ​(δ(Ω′)∣Ω) is the density of next period's inclusive value given today's full industry state. In general it depends on everything in Ω\OmegaΩ: how many models there are, each price and quality, and whatever firms know. The assumption says that it depends on Ω\OmegaΩ only through the current scalar δ(Ω)\delta(\Omega)δ(Ω). Two industry states with the same inclusive value today have the same distribution of the inclusive value tomorrow, and (applying the assumption repeatedly) in all later periods.

What it buys: by Proposition 1 (equations (7) and (8)) the value function depends on Ω\OmegaΩ only through δ\deltaδ, so the state shrinks from the high-dimensional Ω\OmegaΩ to the pair (f0,δ)(f_0,\delta)(f0​,δ) in equations (9) and (10), and the supply side need not be solved. The conditional density can then be written gδ(δ′∣δ)g_{\delta}(\delta'\mid\delta)gδ​(δ′∣δ), and equation (11) gives it a parametric form.

What it rules out: any extra predictive content in Ω\OmegaΩ. A given δ\deltaδ may come from many expensive models or from one cheap model; firms' pricing incentives, and so the future, may differ across the two cases, but the consumer treats them alike. The assumption is on perceptions, so it can be read as bounded rationality. It is also an assumption about an endogenous object: δ\deltaδ contains continuation values, see equation (5), so whether it holds depends on the solution of the model. The paper checks it by adding ln⁡(Jt)\ln(J_t)ln(Jt​) as a second predictor, by the Monte Carlo of equation (12), and by the test in equation (26).

A special case is perfect foresight with δ\deltaδ different in every period: then δ\deltaδ identifies ttt, and the condition holds trivially.

The equation is a fixed-point condition and not an explicit formula, because δ\deltaδ appears on the left and in the conditioning on the right. with ϕ\phiϕ the standard normal density. In the computation the integral is replaced by an average over 20 draws.

The coefficients are not free preference parameters. They are obtained by regressing the model's own sequence δt\delta_tδt​ on its lag, so that perceptions agree on average with what happened (rational expectations within the rule). Since δt\delta_tδt​ depends on V\mathcal{V}V, which depends on (γ1,γ2,σν)(\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\sigma_{\nu})(γ1​,γ2​,σν​), equations (9), (10) and (11) form a joint fixed point. With heterogeneity each consumer type iii has its own (γ1i,γ2i)(\gamma_{1i},\gamma_{2i})(γ1i​,γ2i​).

Iterating the equation forward gives the kkk-step forecast

E[δt+k∣δt]=δˉ+γ2k(δt−δˉ),δˉ≡γ11−γ2E\left[\delta_{t+k}\mid\delta_t\right]=\bar{\delta}+\gamma_2^{k}\left(\delta_t-\bar{\delta}\right),\qquad\bar{\delta}\equiv\frac{\gamma_1}{1-\gamma_2}E[δt+k​∣δt​]=δˉ+γ2k​(δt​−δˉ),δˉ≡1−γ2​γ1​​

For 0<γ2<10<\gamma_2<10<γ2​<1 the consumer expects the market to improve at a decreasing rate toward the asymptote δˉ\bar{\delta}δˉ, which plays the role of a steady state and makes the dynamic program stationary. For example, γ2=0.99\gamma_2=0.99γ2​=0.99 implies that the gap to the asymptote halves about every 69 months. The functional form rules out forecasts that use anything other than δt\delta_tδt​ and rules out, for instance, accelerating improvement; equation (26) tests whether the forecast errors are serially uncorrelated.

This is the data-generating process of the Monte Carlo example in Appendix B of the paper. There is one model per period with a constant price disutility P=5P=5P=5, the discount factor is β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99, and the flow utility ftf_tft​ of the model on sale follows a first-order autoregression that starts at f=−0.04f=-0.04f=−0.04. The consumer knows PPP, the parameters of the process and the current ftf_tft​.

The purpose is to test the forecasting rule of equation (11). Here ftf_tft​ is exactly autoregressive, as in Hendel and Nevo (2006) and Melnikov, but the inclusive value δt\delta_tδt​ is a nonlinear function of ftf_tft​ (it contains the option value of upgrading, see equation (10)) and so is not. A consumer who assumes equation (11) for δ\deltaδ is therefore misspecified. The paper compares her purchase probabilities with those of a consumer who uses the true process, and finds them very close.

This is the vector of sample moments of the GMM estimator. ξ⃗(α,Σ)\vec{\xi}(\alpha,\Sigma)ξ​(α,Σ) stacks the unobserved characteristics ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ over all model-months (4,436 observations). For given parameters it is obtained in two steps: the share inversion of equations (21) and (22) gives F⃗(αp,Σ)\vec{F}(\alpha^p,\Sigma)F(αp,Σ), and then equation (15) gives ξjt=Fjt−xjtαx\xi_{jt}=F_{jt}-x_{jt}\alpha^xξjt​=Fjt​−xjt​αx. The matrix zzz has one row per model-month and one column per instrument, so GGG has one element per instrument: the sample cross-product of that instrument with the structural error.

The identifying assumption is that the instruments are uncorrelated with unobserved quality at the true parameters:

E[zjt′ξjt]=0E\left[z_{jt}'\xi_{jt}\right]=0E[zjt′​ξjt​]=0

Price does not satisfy this, since firms observe ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ before pricing, so price is not in zzz. The instruments are the characteristics xjtx_{jt}xjt​ themselves, the mean characteristics of the same firm's models and of all models in the month, and the number of models of the firm and of all firms. The last three groups shift markups through the closeness of competition and are assumed unrelated to ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ because characteristics and entry are taken as exogenous.

The moments are exactly those of static BLP; the dynamics enter only through the mapping from parameters to ξ⃗\vec{\xi}ξ​. At wrong values of (αp,Σ)(\alpha^p,\Sigma)(αp,Σ) the model needs a ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ that is correlated with the instruments to fit the shares, and GGG is far from zero. Because ξjt\xi_{jt}ξjt​ is linear in αx\alpha^xαx, the moment is linear in αx\alpha^xαx for given F⃗\vec{F}F, which is used in equation (20).

This is the GMM estimator: the parameters minimize a quadratic form in the moments G(α,Σ)G(\alpha,\Sigma)G(α,Σ) of equation (19). WWW is a positive definite weighting matrix that says how the moments are traded off when there are more instruments than parameters; a standard first-stage choice is (z′z)−1(z'z)^{-1}(z′z)−1, and the efficient choice is the inverse of the variance of the moments. The paper's non-nested tests use first-stage estimates.

The minimization separates into a linear and a nonlinear part. For given (αp,Σ)(\alpha^p,\Sigma)(αp,Σ) the inversion yields F⃗\vec{F}F, and ξ⃗=F⃗−xαx\vec{\xi}=\vec{F}-x\alpha^xξ​=F−xαx is linear in αx\alpha^xαx, so the minimizing αx\alpha^xαx is the linear IV formula

α^x(αp,Σ)=(x′zWz′x)−1x′zWz′F⃗(αp,Σ)\hat{\alpha}^x(\alpha^p,\Sigma)=\left(x'zWz'x\right)^{-1}x'zWz'\vec{F}(\alpha^p,\Sigma)α^x(αp,Σ)=(x′zWz′x)−1x′zWz′F(αp,Σ)

Substituting this back leaves a search over αp\alpha^pαp and the diagonal of Σ\SigmaΣ only (three numbers in the base specification: the mean price coefficient and two standard deviations). Each evaluation of the objective requires the whole inner computation: the Bellman equation (9), the inclusive values (10), the forecasting regressions (11), the holdings (17), the shares (18) and the inversion (22), for every simulated type.

The discount factor is not in the parameter vector; it is fixed at β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99 because patience and weak tastes are hard to tell apart. When the micro moment on household penetration is added, GGG gains one more element (the model's change in ownership between September 2002 and September 2005 minus the survey figure), which helps pin down the amount of repurchase and hence Σ\SigmaΣ. Identification requires that the inversion be unique, which the paper imposes as Assumption 2.

This is the share-matching condition, the analogue of the BLP inversion. On the left, sjts_{jt}sjt​ is the observed market share: units of model jjj sold in month ttt divided by the market size, the number of US households. On the right is the model's prediction from equation (18). There is one equation and one unknown FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ for each of the 4,436 model-months, and the solution F⃗(αp,Σ)\vec{F}(\alpha^p,\Sigma)F(αp,Σ) is the vector of mean flow utilities that makes the model fit the sales data exactly, given the nonlinear parameters.

The logic is the same as in static BLP: with a continuum of consumers there is no sampling error in shares, so any gap between the data and the prediction from observables is attributed to unobserved quality, and ξjt=Fjt−xjtαx\xi_{jt}=F_{jt}-x_{jt}\alpha^xξjt​=Fjt​−xjt​αx is recovered from the solution (equation (15)).

Two things differ. First, the system cannot be solved month by month. FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ affects the share of month ttt directly; the shares of later months through the holdings in equation (17), because buyers at ttt carry fijtf_{ijt}fijt​ forward; and the shares of earlier months through expectations, because FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ changes δit\delta_{it}δit​ and so the forecasting rule of equation (11). All 4,436 equations are coupled. Second, uniqueness is not guaranteed. The argument of Berry (1994) needs all products to be substitutes, and here a model today can be a complement to a model two periods ahead through upgrading. The paper assumes uniqueness (Assumption 2) and reports that different starting values always lead to the same solution. The system is solved with the iteration in equation (22).

This is the iteration that solves the share equations (21). If the predicted share of model jjj in month ttt is below the observed share, FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ is raised, and conversely. A vector F⃗\vec{F}F is a fixed point if and only if ln⁡(sjt)=ln⁡[s^jt(F⃗,αp,Σ)]\ln(s_{jt})=\ln[\hat{s}_{jt}(\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)]ln(sjt​)=ln[s^jt​(F,αp,Σ)] for all j,tj,tj,t, so for any ψ≠0\psi\ne0ψ=0 the fixed points are the solutions of equation (21). The tuning parameter ψ\psiψ affects only the step length. In static BLP the step is ψ=1\psi=1ψ=1, and the map is a contraction.

Why ψ=1−β\psi=1-\betaψ=1−β is the natural step here. From equation (16), ln⁡s^ijt=vijt−Vi(fi0t,δit)\ln\hat{s}_{ijt}=v_{ijt}-\mathcal{V}_i(f_{i0t},\delta_{it})lns^ijt​=vijt​−Vi​(fi0t​,δit​), where vijt≡fijt−Pijt+βE[Vi(fijt,δi,t+1)∣δit]v_{ijt}\equiv f_{ijt}-P_{ijt}+\beta E[\mathcal{V}_i(f_{ijt},\delta_{i,t+1})\mid\delta_{it}]vijt​≡fijt​−Pijt​+βE[Vi​(fijt​,δi,t+1​)∣δit​]. Differentiating equation (9), the value function rises with the holding by the expected discounted time the holding is kept, which is at most 1/(1−β)1/(1-\beta)1/(1−β) and close to it when repurchase is rare:

∂vijt∂Fjt=1+β∂E[Vi(fijt,δi,t+1)∣δit]∂fijt≈11−β\frac{\partial v_{ijt}}{\partial F_{jt}}=1+\beta\frac{\partial E\left[\mathcal{V}_i(f_{ijt},\delta_{i,t+1})\mid\delta_{it}\right]}{\partial f_{ijt}}\approx\frac{1}{1-\beta}∂Fjt​∂vijt​​=1+β∂fijt​∂E[Vi​(fijt​,δi,t+1​)∣δit​]​≈1−β1​

Since ∂Vi(fi0t,δit)/∂vijt=s^ijt\partial\mathcal{V}_i(f_{i0t},\delta_{it})/\partial v_{ijt}=\hat{s}_{ijt}∂Vi​(fi0t​,δit​)/∂vijt​=s^ijt​, and holding fixed the holdings and the forecasting rule,

∂ln⁡s^ijt∂Fjt≈1−s^ijt1−β≈11−β\frac{\partial\ln\hat{s}_{ijt}}{\partial F_{jt}}\approx\frac{1-\hat{s}_{ijt}}{1-\beta}\approx\frac{1}{1-\beta}∂Fjt​∂lns^ijt​​≈1−β1−s^ijt​​≈1−β1​

because monthly shares are tiny. A gap of ln⁡(sjt)−ln⁡(s^jt)\ln(s_{jt})-\ln(\hat{s}_{jt})ln(sjt​)−ln(s^jt​) in log shares is therefore closed, to first order, by changing FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ by 1−β1-\beta1−β times the gap. With ψ=1\psi=1ψ=1 the step would be about 100 times too long at β=0.99\beta=0.99β=0.99 and the iteration would overshoot. This supports the note's reading that FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ is a monthly flow while shares respond to its discounted sum; the paper itself gives no reason for the choice.

The paper does not prove that the map is a contraction. Changing FjtF_{jt}Fjt​ also moves shares in other months through equations (11) and (17), which the heuristic ignores. In practice the update is interleaved with a few iterations of equations (9), (10) and (11) until everything converges jointly.

This is how consumer types are simulated. The base draw α~i\tilde{\alpha}_iα~i​ is a vector of independent standard normal variables with density ϕ\phiϕ, one element per coefficient; α\alphaα is the vector of mean coefficients; and Σ1/2\Sigma^{1/2}Σ1/2 is a square root of the variance matrix. The transformation gives the required moments:

E[αi]=α,Var⁡(αi)=Σ1/2E[α~iα~i′](Σ1/2)′=ΣE[\alpha_i]=\alpha,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(\alpha_i)=\Sigma^{1/2}E\left[\tilde{\alpha}_i\tilde{\alpha}_i'\right]\left(\Sigma^{1/2}\right)'=\SigmaE[αi​]=α,Var(αi​)=Σ1/2E[α~i​α~i′​](Σ1/2)′=Σ

so αi\alpha_iαi​ is normal with mean α\alphaα and variance Σ\SigmaΣ, as assumed in equation (14). With the diagonal Σ\SigmaΣ used in the paper, each coefficient is its mean plus its standard deviation times its own base draw. In the base specification only the constant and the price coefficient have nonzero standard deviations, for example a price coefficient with reported mean −3.30-3.30−3.30 and standard deviation 0.3450.3450.345; Table 1 reports the diagonal of Σ1/2\Sigma^{1/2}Σ1/2.

Separating the base draws from the parameters has two uses. First, the same base draws are kept while the optimizer changes (α,Σ)(\alpha,\Sigma)(α,Σ), so the simulated objective in equation (20) is a smooth function of the parameters and does not jump with resampling. Second, integrals over consumers can be written over α~i\tilde{\alpha}_iα~i​ with the fixed density ϕ\phiϕ, as in equation (18), and the importance sampling density of equation (24) is defined on the base draws.

Each simulated type requires its own solution of equations (9), (10) and (11) and its own distribution of holdings, equation (17). Computing time is therefore proportional to the number of types, which is why the paper uses only 40 draws and takes care to choose them well, with Halton sequences and importance sampling.

The aim is to simulate integrals over consumer types, such as equation (18), with few draws. Most types almost never buy, so draws from ϕ\phiϕ waste effort on types that contribute nearly nothing to shares. The standard remedy is to draw from a density proportional to the size of the integrand. Total predicted sales to a type are s^sum(α~i,F⃗,αp,Σ)\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha}_i,\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)s^sum​(α~i​,F,αp,Σ), so the target is proportional to s^sumϕ\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}\phis^sum​ϕ. Dividing by its integral makes it a density:

g(α~i)=s^sum(α~i,F⃗,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~i)∫s^sum(α~,F⃗,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~)dα~,∫g(α~)dα~=1g(\tilde{\alpha}_i)=\frac{\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha}_i,\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)\phi(\tilde{\alpha}_i)}{\int\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha},\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)\phi(\tilde{\alpha})d\tilde{\alpha}},\qquad\int g(\tilde{\alpha})d\tilde{\alpha}=1g(α~i​)=∫s^sum​(α~,F,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~)dα~s^sum​(α~i​,F,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~i​)​,∫g(α~)dα~=1

which is equation (24), the paper's equation (C1).

Sampling from it by acceptance and rejection. Let BBB be an upper bound on s^sum\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}s^sum​. Draw α~\tilde{\alpha}α~ from ϕ\phiϕ and accept it with probability s^sum(α~,F⃗,αp,Σ)/B\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha},\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)/Bs^sum​(α~,F,αp,Σ)/B. and by Bayes' rule the density of an accepted draw is

[s^sum(α~i,F⃗,αp,Σ)/B]ϕ(α~i)Pr⁡(accept)=s^sum(α~i,F⃗,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~i)∫s^sum(α~,F⃗,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~)dα~=g(α~i)\frac{\left[\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha}_i,\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)/B\right]\phi(\tilde{\alpha}_i)}{\Pr(\text{accept})}=\frac{\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha}_i,\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)\phi(\tilde{\alpha}_i)}{\int\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}(\tilde{\alpha},\vec{F},\alpha^p,\Sigma)\phi(\tilde{\alpha})d\tilde{\alpha}}=g(\tilde{\alpha}_i)Pr(accept)[s^sum​(α~i​,F,αp,Σ)/B]ϕ(α~i​)​=∫s^sum​(α~,F,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~)dα~s^sum​(α~i​,F,αp,Σ)ϕ(α~i​)​=g(α~i​)

The bound BBB cancels, so only relative purchase propensities matter: a type is kept in proportion to how much it buys.

The density is fixed before estimation. s^sum\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}s^sum​ is evaluated once, at a preliminary guess of (αp,Σ)(\alpha^p,\Sigma)(αp,Σ) and the F⃗\vec{F}F that solves the share equations (21) at that guess, and the accepted base draws are then held fixed while the optimizer moves. The density oversamples likely buyers, and the weights of equation (25) undo the oversampling. The note's formula agrees with the paper.

∫m(α~)ϕ(α~)dα~≈1R∑i=1Rwim(α~i)\int m(\tilde{\alpha})\phi(\tilde{\alpha})d\tilde{\alpha}\approx\frac{1}{R}\sum_{i=1}^{R}w_im(\tilde{\alpha}_i)∫m(α~)ϕ(α~)dα~≈R1​i=1∑R​wi​m(α~i​)

The second says that for m=s^summ=\hat{s}_{\text{sum}}m=s^sum​ every draw gives the same weighted value, so total sales are simulated with zero variance at the parameter values where ggg was built. Individual model shares, and shares at other parameter values, still have simulation error, but far less than under sampling from ϕ\phiϕ. The weights are computed once together with ggg and held fixed during estimation. The note's formula agrees with the paper.

This is a specification test of the forecasting rule, equation (11), and not part of the estimator. For consumer type iii the forecast error is the residual

νi,t+1=δi,t+1−γ1i−γ2iδit\nu_{i,t+1}=\delta_{i,t+1}-\gamma_{1i}-\gamma_{2i}\delta_{it}νi,t+1​=δi,t+1​−γ1i​−γ2i​δit​

computed from the model's sequence of inclusive values at the estimated parameters. If the autoregression is the correct description of how δit\delta_{it}δit​ evolves, the error has mean zero given everything known at ttt, and νit\nu_{it}νit​ is known at ttt. By iterated expectations,

E[νitνi,t+1]=E[νitE[νi,t+1∣δit,νit]]=0E\left[\nu_{it}\nu_{i,t+1}\right]=E\left[\nu_{it}E\left[\nu_{i,t+1}\mid\delta_{it},\nu_{it}\right]\right]=0E[νit​νi,t+1​]=E[νit​E[νi,t+1​∣δit​,νit​]]=0

which is the equation (the note writes the second subscript as it+1it+1it+1, meaning i,t+1i,t+1i,t+1). If instead consumers' forecasts were systematically wrong for several months in a row, for example because improvement accelerates or because an omitted state variable predicts δ\deltaδ, consecutive errors would be correlated.

The test has content because the least squares regression that produces γ1i\gamma_{1i}γ1i​ and γ2i\gamma_{2i}γ2i​ makes the residuals orthogonal to a constant and to δit\delta_{it}δit​ by construction, but not to the lagged residual. The moment is not imposed in estimation; it is evaluated afterwards. For the median consumer its sample value is −0.474-0.474−0.474 with a standard deviation of 2.952.952.95, a ratio of about −0.16-0.16−0.16, so the null hypothesis of no serial correlation cannot be rejected. Note the direction of the statement: the paper fails to reject the absence of serial correlation, and it does not say that serial correlation is present. The test supports the rational expectations reading of equation (11), together with the robustness check that adds ln⁡(Jt)\ln(J_t)ln(Jt​) as a second predictor.

This is the chained Laspeyres price index in the style of the BLS, the paper's equation (13). The numerator is the cost at month t+1t+1t+1 prices of the basket bought in month ttt, with quantities proportional to the month-ttt shares sjts_{jt}sjt​; the denominator is its cost at month-ttt prices. The ratio is the one-month price relative, and the index is the product of these relatives from March 2000, where I=100I=100I=100. Models are linked over time by name. For a model that exits, pj,t+1p_{j,t+1}pj,t+1​ is not observed: the BLS-style version imputes the average price change of continuing models, and the Pakes version predicts it from a monthly hedonic regression. The two indices fall to 12.7 and 14.5.

The index takes the basket as given and asks what it costs later. It is therefore silent about who is buying and how much they value the good, which is the point of the comparison with the dynamic index.

Conversion to dollars per household. The paper adds the outside good to the basket with a constant price, multiplies the resulting index by the initial share-weighted average price of 961 dollars, divides by 100 and subtracts the result from 961. Writing ItoI^{o}_tIto​ for the index with the outside good included, the cost-of-living measure is

961×(1−Ito100)961\times\left(1-\frac{I^{o}_t}{100}\right)961×(1−100Ito​​)

the amount by which income could fall while the first-period basket remains affordable. Because nearly all households buy nothing in a given month, each month adds roughly the saving on that month's basket,

∑j=1Jtsjt(pjt−pj,t+1)\sum_{j=1}^{J_t}s_{jt}\left(p_{jt}-p_{j,t+1}\right)j=1∑Jt​​sjt​(pjt​−pj,t+1​)

per household, a small share times a price cut; this approximation is a reading of the construction and is not displayed in the paper. It explains why the measure reaches only 1.74 dollars (1.72 for the Pakes version) and why it keeps rising as prices fall and sales grow.

The dynamic index instead finds the state-contingent tax that keeps average flow utility constant, with a buyer charged the amortized price (1−β)pjt(1-\beta)p_{jt}(1−β)pjt​ in every later period. It uses the linear-price specification, which is column 4 of the paper's Table 2 (the paper's text says column 3, but column 3 is the model with extra random coefficients). It ends at 1.27 dollars and is concave in time, because later buyers have lower valuations or already own a camcorder.
